The strongest founder picks that are live and verified today are SiteGuru at $79 for SEO and AI-search visibility, FlexiFunnels at $49 for landing pages and funnels, Cleanlist AI at $79 for verified lead data, SendFox at $29 for email, and TidyCal at $29 for booking sales and demo calls. Each one carries a money-back window printed on its own deal page, so you can test it in your real business before you commit. Read that line, because AppSumo sets the window per listing and it is not always 60 days. Prices below were checked on appsumo.com on July 10, 2026, and lifetime deals rotate fast, so confirm the price on the page before you buy.
- [GoHighLevel SaaS Mode in 2026: How to Resell GoHighLevel as Your Own Software](https://imisofts.com/blog/gohighlevel-saas-mode-2026/): Short answer: GoHighLevel SaaS Mode lets you resell the entire platform, white-labeled under your own brand, on the $497 per month Agency Pro plan. The break-even is two to three resold clients, you keep 100 percent of what you charge, and rebilling turns your clients' text and email usage into a second stream of profit. But it is not passive income. You are effectively becoming a small software company, with onboarding, support, and churn to manage, and most resellers take 12 to 18 months to reach real profit. Turn it on if you already have clients (or a clear plan to get them) and will treat it like a business. Skip it if you just want a CRM for yourself. This guide covers what SaaS Mode is, how it works, what it costs, the reseller math, the setup steps, and the honest downsides.
- [How to Scrape Leads With Apify in 2026 (Step-by-Step Guide)](https://imisofts.com/blog/how-to-scrape-leads-with-apify/): Short answer: to scrape leads with Apify, create a free account, choose a ready-made scraper (called an Actor) that matches where your leads live, configure a specific search, run it, then enrich and verify the results before you send anything. For local businesses the go-to is the Google Maps Scraper; for B2B roles and companies you use a LinkedIn or B2B-database Actor. Your first run takes about 15 minutes and costs nothing on the free $5 monthly credit, which is enough for roughly 500 to 1,000 leads. The honest catch: Apify hands you raw data, not deliverability or legal cover. The money is in how tightly you target, how well you verify, and how compliantly you reach out. Here is the exact workflow we use.

### Founder's playbook (AI agents, calling, compliance, operations) (69)

- [Telemarketing Sales Rule: 5 Years of Records, Not Two](https://imisofts.com/blog/telemarketing-sales-rule/): What does the Telemarketing Sales Rule make you keep? Since 16 May 2024, 16 CFR 310.5 has required sellers and telemarketers to keep most of the listed records for 5 years, up from two, including a record of each telemarketing call (required from 15 October 2024) and a copy of each unique prerecorded message. When I read the FTC’s own compliance guide on 13 November 2026, its recordkeeping section still said “two years”. My view: a policy built from that guide is three years short. The rule covers telemarketing, which 16 CFR 310.2(ii) defines as a plan, program or campaign to induce a purchase or a charitable contribution by telephone that “involves more than one interstate telephone call”. Most B2B calls are exempt (see below).
- [GDPR Data Retention Period: None Set, CNIL Guide Says 3 Years](https://imisofts.com/blog/gdpr-data-retention-period/): What is the GDPR data retention period? The GDPR’s text sets no fixed number. Article 5(1)(e) says personal data must be kept in a form which permits identification for no longer than is necessary for the purposes it is processed for, and the UK’s ICO says the UK GDPR “does not set specific time limits for different types of data.” For a prospect who is not a customer, France’s CNIL, in a 2021 reference framework that is not binding, says the data may be kept for three years from its collection or from the prospect’s last contact, and that opening an email should not be considered contact (my translation). In my view, the bigger risk in outbound is not deleting too early. It is keeping every lead you ever imported with no end date at all.
- [Branded Caller ID Cost: $0.075 to $0.12 a Call at 3 Vendors](https://imisofts.com/blog/branded-caller-id-cost/): How much does branded caller ID cost? On the pricing pages and docs I read on 11 November 2026, Telnyx charges $0.075 per call that displays your brand plus $50 once and $50 a month per brand, Retell adds $0.10 per outbound call, and Twilio charges $0.12 a call, billed only when the brand information is delivered. Twilio and Telnyx list two US networks for it, T-Mobile and Verizon. My view: branded caller ID is a per-call fee for a better first impression. Retell itself says a branded call may still be marked “Spam Likely” without its separate verified-number service.
- [DSAR Response Time: One Month, and the Data Source Question](https://imisofts.com/blog/dsar-response-time/): How long do you have to answer a DSAR? Under the UK and EU GDPR, without undue delay and at the latest within one month, extendable by two further months where necessary, given the complexity and number of the requests, if you tell the person why within that first month. Under California’s CCPA, if it applies to your business, 45 calendar days, extendable once by 45 more. For UK requests received from 5 February 2026, the clock can pause for clarification you reasonably require. My view: after a cold email, the request often won’t say “subject access request.” It may just say “where did you get my email?”
- [Do Not Call List for Businesses: The Owner’s Cell Is the Catch](https://imisofts.com/blog/do-not-call-list-for-businesses/): Can a business be on the Do Not Call list? In the US, not as a business line. The FTC says that the National Do Not Call Registry “is for personal phone numbers. Business phone numbers and fax lines are not covered,” and most calls made to solicit sales from a business are exempt from its do-not-call rules. The catch is the owner’s cell phone: on 12 October 2022 the Ninth Circuit held, at the motion-to-dismiss stage, that the plaintiffs’ registered cell phones used for both personal and business purposes are presumptively residential. My view: “business numbers are exempt” holds for a switchboard and can fail on a scraped list, like the one alleged in that case.
- [Email Suppression List: Why You Should Not Delete Opt-Outs](https://imisofts.com/blog/email-suppression-list/): An email suppression list is the record of people who told you to stop, kept so that no later import or bought list puts them back into a sequence. My suggestion, based mainly on UK regulator guidance and a French regulator recommendation: do not delete it. The UK regulator’s right to object guidance (page last updated 2 November 2026) says: “You should not delete a person's information from a suppression list.” In the US, once someone opts out through your opt-out mechanism, CAN-SPAM bars you from selling or transferring their address except to comply with the law. My view: the riskiest opt-out is the one someone deleted. A tool’s re-entry block, where it has one, covers that tool only, so the next bought or scraped list can bring the address straight back.
- [Perplexity SEO Audit: About 4,310 Bot Fetches, 2 Sessions](https://imisofts.com/blog/perplexity-seo/): For Perplexity SEO, Perplexity’s own advice starts with access. Its crawler documentation page recommends allowing PerplexityBot in robots.txt and permitting requests from its published IP ranges “to ensure your site appears in search results”; the list held 13 ranges when I read it on 5 November 2026. Then audit what arrives under that name. In the 30 days to 5 November 2026, Cloudflare counted about 4,310 successful responses to requests it labeled PerplexityBot on imisofts.com, and requests carrying the name also asked for .env files. In the 28 days to 4 November, GA4 credited perplexity.ai with 2 sessions. My view: Perplexity SEO should start with the crawl report, not with content. The mistake I want to avoid is reading a busy PerplexityBot line as progress, then letting anything that calls itself PerplexityBot through the firewall.
- [TCPA Compliance Checklist: 12 Checks Before an AI Agent Dials](https://imisofts.com/blog/tcpa-compliance-checklist/): A TCPA compliance checklist for sales calls has 12 checks, drawn from 47 CFR 64.1200 and the FCC’s caller ID rule (read on 4 November 2026). The core: prior express written consent before an AI or autodialed sales call to a cell phone, telephone solicitations to residential subscribers only from 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time, a Do Not Call Registry version no more than 31 days old for the safe harbor, and opt-outs honored within 10 business days at most. Under 47 U.S.C. 227, a robocall violation can cost $500 or the actual monetary loss, if greater, and up to three times that if willful or knowing. In my view, a TCPA checklist without dates is a liability, and the bigger mistake is treating compliance as a consent form. The consent rules moved twice in 2025, and the revocation rule moves again on 25 November 2026.
- [CAN-SPAM Penalties: Up to $53,088 an Email, and Who Can Sue](https://imisofts.com/blog/can-spam-penalties/): CAN-SPAM penalties run up to $53,088 for each email that breaks the law, the FTC’s maximum civil penalty in 16 CFR 1.98 (current eCFR text, read on 3 November 2026). That is a maximum, not a price: in August 2024 the FTC called its $2.95 million penalty against Verkada the largest it had obtained for a CAN-SPAM violation. States can also claim up to $250 per unlawful email to their residents, affected internet access services up to $25 or $100, and some practices are crimes. In my view, the mistake is pricing your risk off one number: multiplying $53,088 by your list, or deciding nobody gets fined for cold email. The FTC’s compliance guide says “The law makes no exception for business-to-business email.”
- [Reassigned Numbers Database Cost: $8 Buys 1,000 Checks](https://imisofts.com/blog/reassigned-numbers-database/): The FCC’s Reassigned Numbers Database (RND) is not free. On the RND’s interim price table, read on 2 November 2026, checks cost from $8 for 1,000 a month (0.8 cents each), and one-month blocks run up to $28,000 for 50 million (0.056 cents each). It is the only lookup tied to the TCPA safe harbor for reassigned numbers in 47 CFR 64.1200(m): if you had consent, queried the most recent data with your consent date, got a “no” and called because that “no” was wrong, you are not liable under the FCC’s autodialer and artificial or prerecorded voice consent rules. The burden of proof and persuasion is yours. The mistake to avoid is treating a phone validation or carrier lookup, which is a commercial database, as that check. In its December 2018 order (FCC 18-177), the FCC wrote: “We also decline to extend the safe harbor to other commercial databases.”
- [Legitimate Interest Assessment for Cold Email: 3 Tests, 1 Gate](https://imisofts.com/blog/legitimate-interest-assessment/): A legitimate interest assessment (LIA) is the written record of the three-part test (purpose, necessity and balancing) you run before relying on legitimate interests under Article 6(1)(f) of the GDPR. The ICO says the UK GDPR does not require one, “But you should do one anyway.” Since 5 February 2026, when Article 6(11) came fully into force, the UK GDPR has listed processing for direct marketing as an example of a possible legitimate interest. For cold email the LIA only counts after a gate: where the UK’s PECR requires consent for the email, the ICO says legitimate interests cannot be your lawful basis. The mistake is treating the LIA as permission to send. As the ICO puts it, “Legitimate interests can’t legitimise unlawful processing,” so run the gate first, then the three tests.
- [TCPA Opt-Out Requirements: Pick Your Method From November 25](https://imisofts.com/blog/tcpa-opt-out-requirements/): From 25 November 2026, a business may name the only opt-out methods it has to honor for its robocalls and texts: an automated voice or key press opt-out on the call, reply words such as STOP, or a website or phone number it designates, as long as every call or text discloses them. Requests must still be honored within 10 business days. If your AI agent sells, that buys you little: the FCC’s order leaves the opt-out an artificial-voice sales call owes exactly as it was. The order was published in the Federal Register on 26 October 2026, but until 25 November the rule in force still says callers “may not designate an exclusive means” to revoke consent. On 27 October, Google’s AI Overview for “tcpa opt out requirements” told me callers “may designate” exclusive opt-out methods, in the present tense.
- [CAN-SPAM Unsubscribe Rules: 10 Business Days, Not One Click](https://imisofts.com/blog/can-spam-unsubscribe-requirements/): CAN-SPAM does not require one-click unsubscribe, or even a link. It requires a working reply address or other Internet-based opt-out, shown clearly in every commercial email, that keeps working for 30 days after you send, and it gives you 10 business days to stop emailing anyone who uses it. One-click is Google’s and Yahoo’s rule for bulk senders, and both want those requests honored within two days. On 26 October 2026 I asked Google whether CAN-SPAM requires one-click unsubscribe, and its AI Overview answered yes. That mistake cuts both ways for a cold email team. A plain-text sequence with no opt-out line breaks the law even though it has no links, and a sequence that says “reply stop” needs someone reading the replies in every one of its 40 sending inboxes.
- [Do Not Call Registry Cost: $85 per Area Code, in Your Name](https://imisofts.com/blog/do-not-call-registry-cost/): From 1 October 2026, the National Do Not Call Registry costs a seller $85 a year for each area code after the first five, which are free, up to $23,425 for every area code. The fee is owed by the seller, not by its dialer. A dialer or agency may pay it on the seller’s behalf, but the subscription account must be the seller’s own, and splitting one between clients is banned. A company whose every call is exempt, such as calls to people who signed a written agreement to be called, can register as an Exempt Organization and pay nothing. Your dialer can run the scrub. It cannot own the list for you. Retell’s terms, updated 7 October 2026, say the customer “is responsible for maintaining an active subscription to the Registry”, and smrtPhone’s help center says the dialer “does not issue or manage SANs”.
- [Cloudflare Block AI Bots: Choosing Block Now Stops Googlebot](https://imisofts.com/blog/cloudflare-block-ai-bots/): If your site runs on Cloudflare, the setting to check is the one for AI training. Since 15 September 2026, choosing Block for Training also stops Googlebot, Bingbot and Applebot, so the click meant to keep your pages out of AI models also shuts out the crawlers behind Google, Bing and Apple search. Disallow is the option Cloudflare built to refuse training and keep search. All three AI bot controls come with every Cloudflare plan, Free included, and Cloudflare says 17% of its sites block training in some way, while fewer than 1% block search. Advice written before that date describes a different switch. Until then, the one-click Block AI bots option skipped crawlers that do search and training at once, so it never touched Googlebot. Block, as Cloudflare defines it now, does not skip them, and Cloudflare says more than 20% of web domains sit behind it.
- [GDPR Representative for Cold Email: Weekly Is Not Occasional](https://imisofts.com/blog/gdpr-representative-cold-email/): If your company has no office in the EU and you cold email people there, GDPR Article 27 requires you to name a representative in the EU, in writing, and the UK GDPR has the same rule for prospects in the UK. The one exemption open to a business is for occasional processing, which the European Data Protection Board reads as not regular and outside your normal course of business, so weekly outbound does not fit it. The small-company plans I priced on 21 October 2026 cost €150 to €1,920 a year. Locatefamily.com was fined €525,000 in the Netherlands for having no representative there. It is easy to treat GDPR for cold email as one question: may I send this? That answer mostly sits in each country’s electronic marketing rules, covered in which cold email law applies to you. Article 27 asks something else: once a person in Europe sits in your CRM, who in Europe answers for you?
- [Google Workspace Sending Limits: 2,000 a Day, 500 on Trial](https://imisofts.com/blog/google-workspace-sending-limits/): Each paid Google Workspace user can send 2,000 messages a day, to at most 10,000 recipients in total, 3,000 of them outside your primary domain and 2,000 of those unique, counted over a rolling 24 hours. A trial account gets 500 messages and 500 unique outside recipients a day, and Google’s limits page says a converted trial’s limits rise once the domain has paid at least $100 in total, which can take up to 75 days after that. I read every Google page quoted here on 20 October 2026. It is tempting to start from the 2,000 and multiply it by seats. That is the wrong number to plan around. The inboxes we set up send 20 to 30 cold emails a day each, so the cap never comes close. What decides a Google build is the 500 a new account starts on, the rules for what counts against a user, and one sentence in Google’s acceptable use policy that can cost you the whole account.
- [Are Mortgage Trigger Leads Illegal? Who Can Still Buy Them](https://imisofts.com/blog/mortgage-trigger-leads/): No. Mortgage trigger leads are still legal, but since early March 2026 a credit bureau may sell one only to the lender that made or services the borrower’s current mortgage, a bank or credit union where the borrower has a current account, or a buyer that certifies it has the borrower’s authorization. That is the Homebuyers Privacy Protection Act, Public Law 119-36. The GAO’s report of 6 October 2026 estimates that before it, at most 3.5% of homebuyers may have got their loan through an offer based on a trigger lead. I read every source quoted here on 19 October 2026. When I searched the question, Google’s AI Overview began: “Yes, mortgage trigger leads are largely illegal under federal law.” That reading would send a loan officer looking for a new list. The law is narrower.
- [CAN-SPAM Address Requirement: When a PO Box or Mailbox Counts](https://imisofts.com/blog/can-spam-address-requirement/): Yes, CAN-SPAM accepts a PO box or a virtual mailbox, as long as the US Postal Service can tie it to you. The FTC’s rule lists three valid addresses: your current street address, a Post Office box you have accurately registered with the USPS, or a private mailbox you have accurately registered with a commercial mail receiving agency under USPS rules. The smallest USPS box costs $31 to $170 for six months, and the FTC puts the penalty at up to $53,088 for each email that breaks the law. I read every rule quoted here on 16 October 2026. The easy mistake is treating the footer address as decoration, so a founder working from home prints the home address on every email or pastes in a virtual office address without asking how it is registered. The first is a privacy cost. The second can fail the rule, which asks one thing of a box: can the Postal Service say who rents it?
- [Bland AI Pricing: $0.14 a Minute Until Your 101st Call a Day](https://imisofts.com/blog/bland-ai-pricing/): Bland AI costs $0.14 a minute on its Start plan, which has no monthly fee, or $299 a month plus $0.12 a minute on Build; Enterprise is priced by quote. Unless your calls run long, your call count decides which one you pay: Start stops at 100 calls a day, 100 an hour and 10 at once, and Build at 2,000 a day. I read every price here on Bland’s pricing page and billing docs on 15 October 2026. The per-minute rate is the headline, and the obvious move is to set it against Vapi’s pricing and Retell’s and take the cheapest minute; Bland’s own FAQ invites exactly that comparison. But between Bland’s Start and Build plans the rate moves by two cents. The 101st call of the day adds a $299 monthly fee.
- [How Long Does Google Take to Index a New Page? I Timed 136](https://imisofts.com/blog/how-long-does-google-take-to-index-a-page/): On my site, a new page now shows up in Google Search the day it goes live or the next day: 95 of the 99 pages I published between 7 and 30 September 2026 did. Pages Google has not picked up can wait for weeks. The 37 I published from 31 August to 5 September took a median of 18 days, and most were shown within a day of the indexing request I finally sent. Google’s own guidance says crawling can take anywhere from a few days to a few weeks. That range is Google’s answer, and the same page tells you to be patient. My data is not a range. It splits in two: the next day, or weeks later, with almost nothing in between. If your new page has not been shown by day two, my numbers say it is probably stuck, not slow, and waiting another month is the mistake.
- [Microsoft SMTP AUTH Basic Auth Deprecation: What Breaks in December](https://imisofts.com/blog/smtp-auth-basic-authentication-deprecation/): Microsoft will switch off Basic authentication for SMTP AUTH by default in existing Exchange Online tenants at the end of December 2026. Admins can still turn it back on, tenants created after December 2026 will not have it by default, and Microsoft says it will announce the final removal date in the second half of 2027. Anything that logs in to smtp.office365.com with a username and password is on the affected path; OAuth is the method Microsoft names as supported. It is easy to read that as the end of SMTP for Outlook inboxes. It is not. The Authenticated SMTP box you ticked to connect them to your sequencer is not what Microsoft is switching off. The password login is. If your inboxes went in through a Microsoft sign-in screen, this change is not aimed at them. If they went in as a list of usernames and passwords, it is.
- [Is Cold Email From a Secondary Domain Legal? The Registration Decides](https://imisofts.com/blog/cold-email-secondary-domain-legal/): Yes, if the email says who sent it and the registration tells the truth. None of the US, UK, EU, Canadian or Australian rules I read cares whether you send from your main domain or a secondary one, and consent rules apply as they always did. In the US, the criminal line for the domain itself is the registration: under 18 U.S.C. § 1037, knowingly registering two or more domains under a false identity, then sending more than 100 commercial emails a day from them, carries up to a year in prison, and up to three once a day’s volume passes 2,500. Every email infrastructure build we run starts with sending domains that are not the client’s main one, so the company domain is never at risk. That puts the legal question on every build, and the answer is rarely about the domain.
- [Can an AI Receptionist Answer in Spanish? Give It Its Own Line](https://imisofts.com/blog/ai-receptionist-spanish/): Yes, an AI receptionist can answer in Spanish, but the one built into your field service software may not: ServiceTitan’s voice agent, sold at $2.75 a call, could only understand and respond in English until its spring 2026 release, Housecall Pro’s own CSR AI overview lists Spanish among features coming soon, and Jobber’s receptionist pages do not name a language at all. None of the AI pricing pages I read lists an extra charge for Spanish. What decides the result is routing, and the most accurate setup is an agent that only speaks Spanish, reached on its own number. Smith.ai sells Spanish as a bilingual answering service and RingCentral as multilingual conversational support. Retell’s documentation spells out the trade-off on its own platform: one agent listening for English and Spanish runs on a speech pipeline that is less accurate in each language than a single-language agent.
- [How to Correct an AI Overview: The Report Button Is Not the Fix](https://imisofts.com/blog/how-to-correct-ai-overview/): You cannot edit a Google AI Overview or a ChatGPT answer about your business. Google offers a thumbs-down button and a Report a problem link, and OpenAI takes correction requests through a privacy portal meant for “people whose personal data appears in ChatGPT responses.” What you can change is the page an answer was built from, and, when the false claim sits on no page at all, the written record of what you reported, which is what a federal judge in Chicago weighed on 14 September 2026. The instinct is to treat a wrong AI answer like a wrong listing: find the page that said it and get it changed. In the two court cases I read this month, the answers said things the pages they cited did not, and the reports filed did not stop the answers. They built a record, and in Chicago that record mattered.
- [Vapi vs Retell: The Price Is Close. The Contracts Are Not.](https://imisofts.com/blog/vapi-vs-retell/): Vapi and Retell sit in the same price range per minute, so choose on the contract. Retell’s pay as you go plan includes a BAA you can self-sign at no additional fee and terms that name a 99.5% uptime target, while Vapi charges $2,000 a month for its BAA and puts its first uptime SLA, 99%, on a package with a $999 monthly minimum. Pick Retell for one self-serve contract covering HIPAA, uptime and the calling rules, and Vapi if your engineers want control of every layer and you can pay for the paperwork. Google’s AI Overview for “vapi vs retell” compares setup speed, flexibility, telephony features and pricing structure. On 7 October 2026 I read the contracts instead: both companies’ terms of service, pricing pages, trust centers and compliance docs.
- [Microsoft 365 Sending Limits: A New Tenant Gets 10% for 30 Days](https://imisofts.com/blog/microsoft-365-sending-limits/): A Microsoft 365 mailbox can send to 10,000 recipients a day, but every mailbox in the tenant shares one cap on outside recipients: 500 times the email license count to the power 0.7, plus 9,500, which Microsoft puts at 12,006 a day for 10 licenses. Since mid-September 2026 Microsoft has been rolling out a cut for young tenants: a tenant under 31 days old gets 10 percent of that cap and one aged 31 to 60 days gets 25 percent, and the rollout is expected to finish by the end of November 2026. Multiply 25 Outlook inboxes by 10,000 and a cold email setup looks limitless. It is not. On 6 October 2026 I read Microsoft’s limits pages, four Exchange team posts and Message Center post MC1454397, and the meter that matters now runs per tenant, by license count and by age.
- [Bing AI Performance Report: Copilot's Top Ten Is Not Google's](https://imisofts.com/blog/bing-ai-performance-report/): Bing’s AI Performance report shows how often Microsoft Copilot, Bing’s AI summaries and select partner AI apps cite your pages, which pages they cite and the grounding queries behind them. On imisofts.com, from 16 to 28 September 2026, the ten pages Copilot cited most and the ten pages Google sent the most clicks shared no page at all. If you only read Search Console, you do not know which of your pages Copilot is citing. On 14 September I published the opposite result for Google: nine of the ten pages its AI features showed most on my site already earned clicks, so AEO and SEO were the same job. That was a Google finding. It did not survive Bing.
- [Can You Keep Your Number After Canceling an AI Receptionist?](https://imisofts.com/blog/cancel-ai-receptionist-keep-number/): Yes, if you port the number to another carrier before you cancel, or it already sits in a carrier account in your name. Cancel first and you can lose it. Twilio lets you reclaim a released number for 10 days, closing a Twilio account stops calls at once and deletes its data in 30 days, and Vapi says its free numbers cannot be ported to another carrier at all. Your call recordings need the same order: export them before the account closes. I read pages from the help centers, docs and terms of Twilio, Telnyx, Vapi, Retell and Bland, plus the FCC’s porting guide, on 1 October 2026. When we scope AI call answering for home services, the exit goes in the plan early: the agent can be rebuilt elsewhere; the number can only be moved.
- [Can an AI Agent Call Law Firm Leads? Rule 7.3 Asks Who Started the Call](https://imisofts.com/blog/ai-intake-law-firm-solicitation-rules/): Yes, when the lead asked first. An AI intake agent that calls back a person who filled in your form is answering a request, and the ABA’s own comment says a communication made “in response to a request for information” is not a solicitation. The same agent dialing an accident victim from a police report is a solicitation by real-time voice, which Model Rule 7.3(b) bans and which Texas Rule 7.03 names outright as “electronically interactive” contact made “on behalf of a lawyer”. I read both texts and their comments on 28 September 2026 because every AI intake build for a law firm starts with the same request: call every new lead back inside a minute. Whether the agent may do that is decided by a rule written for humans, and the rule is clearer than the debate around it.
- [Do You Have to Port Your Number to Use an AI Receptionist? No. Forward It](https://imisofts.com/blog/port-number-to-ai-receptionist/): No. You do not have to port your business number to use an AI receptionist. Forward the number to the line the agent answers on, every call or only the calls you miss, and the agent is live in one star code. Port later, if ever, and then to a carrier you control, not into the vendor's number pool. I read the porting and forwarding pages of Twilio, Telnyx, Vapi, Retell, Bland, HighLevel, Smith.ai, Verizon and the FCC on 28 September 2026, because it is one of the first questions a trades owner asks when we scope AI calling for home services.
- [Can an AI Receptionist Take Card Payments? The Recording Is the Risk](https://imisofts.com/blog/ai-receptionist-card-payments/): Yes, an AI receptionist can take a card payment over the phone. What gets a business into trouble is not the AI hearing the number, it is the recording and the transcript that keep it: PCI DSS Requirement 3.3.1 bans storing a card's security code after authorization, and the PCI Security Standards Council says a CVV kept in a .wav or .mp3 file after authorization breaks that rule. So the question for a vendor is not "are you PCI compliant" but "what happens to the recording while the caller reads the card". I read the four platforms' own pages on 25 September 2026 for this piece, because I build these agents for trades businesses through our AI calling for home services work, and a deposit over the phone is a request I hear from trades owners.
- [AI SDR Disclosure: CAN-SPAM Asks Who Sent It, LinkedIn Bans the Bot](https://imisofts.com/blog/ai-sdr-disclosure/): CAN-SPAM does not make your AI SDR admit it is a machine. The made-up name it signs with is the bigger exposure, and on LinkedIn the disclosure question barely matters, because the platform bans the bot. That is the short answer from the texts I read on 24 September 2026. CAN-SPAM asks whether an email identifies the business that sent it, not whether a human typed it. California’s bot law is written for public-facing websites and apps, including social networks, which puts LinkedIn inside it more clearly than email. LinkedIn’s own User Agreement forbids bots sending messages at all. And since 2 August 2026, the EU AI Act has required AI systems that talk directly to people to say so. I build cold email infrastructure, so I read these from the sending side.

That is not where a promise lives. If the platform behind your AI receptionist goes down, your phone stops ringing and nobody owes you the job you lost. I read the pricing pages and the public terms of three AI voice platforms on 23 September 2026. Only one of the three puts an uptime figure inside the contract you actually sign, and none of the three publishes a service credit for missing it. The layer underneath them, the telephony provider, publishes both, and that is where the protection you can actually buy is sitting. The agency half mostly does not. If your AEO quote is $2,500 and it tracks a hundred prompts, you are buying about $189 of software and $2,311 of somebody’s time. That second number is the whole conversation, and it stays folded inside the first. I run AI search optimization for clients, so this is an awkward thing for me to publish. - [Lead Scraper Cost: The Blocked Requests Nobody Quotes You For](https://imisofts.com/blog/lead-scraper-cost/): A lead scraper's price is not set by how many pages you pull. On ZenRows' published rates, one balance of 250,000 credits fetches about 250,000 plain pages or about 10,000 well defended ones. Same plan, same money, twenty five times the yield. - [Which Cold Email Law Applies to You? The Inbox Decides](https://imisofts.com/blog/which-cold-email-law-applies-to-you/): The law that governs a cold email is the law of the inbox it lands in, not the law of the country your company is registered in. Australia, Canada and the European Union each publish an explicit territorial test for marketing email, and on all three the recipient's side alone is enough to trigger it. Founders ask me whether cold email is legal where they are based, as though that settles it. I have built outbound infrastructure across 500+ projects in 30 countries, and I have never once seen a list that respects a border. The company is in one country, the domains are registered in another, the sending servers are in a third, and the recipients are spread across twenty. There is no single "our law" in that picture, and the one jurisdiction that almost never decides the answer is your own.

- [Google OAuth Verification: One Setting Skips the Security Audit](https://imisofts.com/blog/google-oauth-verification-restricted-scopes/): Google sorts every OAuth scope into three levels, and the level decides your whole timeline. Non-sensitive scopes need basic verification. Sensitive scopes add a review Google's own table puts at ten business days. Restricted scopes, which include reading a Gmail inbox, add a third-party security assessment that you pay for, wait six weeks for, and repeat every year. If the app runs inside one Google Workspace organisation and the user type is set to Internal, Google says restricted scopes do not require further review at all. Google publishes the table, on the Workspace guide for configuring the consent screen, last updated 3 September 2026. Three columns: basic app verification, additional app verification, security assessment. Non-sensitive scopes tick the first. Sensitive scopes tick two. Restricted scopes tick all three.

- [Can You Opt Out by Talking to an AI Voice Agent? Yes. Your Stack Drops It.](https://imisofts.com/blog/ai-voice-agent-opt-out/): Yes. Under 47 CFR 64.1200(a)(10) a person may revoke consent by using any reasonable method to clearly express a desire not to receive further calls, and you have ten business days to honor it. Saying it out loud to your AI agent qualifies, and the same paragraph bars you from making a keypress or a text reply the only way out. But the automatic opt-out machinery in almost every calling stack lives on the text channel. The voice channel has a microphone and no destination. Almost every operator I speak to believes the platform has this covered, because they have watched it work. It does work, on SMS. - [Search Generative AI Control: Do Not Switch It Off Blind](https://imisofts.com/blog/search-generative-ai-control/): Google's Search generative AI control is a Search Console setting that decides whether your site can appear in AI Overviews, AI Mode and generative AI features in Google Discover. Google rolled it out to all websites worldwide on August 31, 2026, and the default on every property is Include. Set it to Exclude and your links and content are prevented from appearing in those features, and Google states you will not receive any traffic or impressions from them. Every founder I have shown this setting to reaches for Exclude inside about four seconds. Do not. - [California AI Caller Disclosure: A Human Has to Say It First](https://imisofts.com/blog/california-ai-caller-disclosure-law/): California does require you to tell people your caller uses an artificial voice. Almost every AI calling stack I have reviewed gets the disclosure wrong, and not because it is missing. It is in the wrong mouth. The requirement lives in Public Utilities Code Section 2874, which was amended by AB 2905 in September 2024. It sits as item three inside an announcement that the statute says must be an unrecorded, natural voice announcement made to the person called by the person calling. Read literally, your AI agent cannot introduce itself. In California the answer is yes, and it is the least interesting part of the sentence.

- [Does llms.txt Actually Work? - [CAN-SPAM Liability: Your Cold Email Agency Cannot Absorb It](https://imisofts.com/blog/cold-email-agency-liability/): Your cold email agency cannot take on your legal risk. There is no clause, indemnity or master services agreement that moves it, because the FTC wrote the rule specifically to stop that from working. Under the CAN-SPAM Act, both the company whose product is promoted in a commercial email and the company that actually sends it may be held legally responsible. The FTC states in its own compliance guide for business that even if you hire another company to handle your email marketing, you cannot contract away your legal responsibility to comply with the law. Hiring an agency adds a second liable party. It does not remove the first one.
- [Can You Charge Clients for n8n? Yes, Until Their Credentials Enter Your Instance.](https://imisofts.com/blog/can-you-charge-clients-for-n8n/): The riskiest object in your n8n build is not a workflow. It is the API key your client handed you. Yes, you can charge clients for n8n work. n8n's own license documentation lists building workflows, providing consulting services and setting up or maintaining n8n as allowed, and n8n deliberately removed the older clause that blocked exactly that. What is not allowed is white-labeling n8n and offering it to your customers for money, or hosting n8n and charging people to access it. The boundary is not whether you invoice. It is whether your customers connect their own accounts to an instance you run.

- [When to Hire an n8n Developer: Count Failure Modes, Not Workflows.](https://imisofts.com/blog/when-to-hire-an-n8n-developer/): Nobody needs a developer to build an n8n workflow. That is the entire point of n8n, and anyone quoting you by the workflow is charging you for the easy part. Hire an n8n developer when your workflows write, spend money, or contact a human, not when you have a lot of them. Building in n8n is deliberately easy, so the node count and the workflow count tell you almost nothing about what the work costs. What it cannot do is quote a rate, recommend coverage or talk through terms, because those activities require a licensed human under federal mortgage rules and state insurance law no matter who performs them. - [Do You Need a GoHighLevel Developer? What you need is someone who has already built the specific system you are describing and can show it to you working, not someone who bills by the hour to learn on your account. So the real question is not developer or no developer. It is proof or no proof. Decide the outcome you want, a white-label SaaS, an AI follow-up system, a snapshot you can clone across locations, then make the person prove they have shipped that exact thing before you hand over a login. That one filter matters more than any hourly rate on any marketplace.
- [AI Voice Agents Won't Get Your Real Estate Team Sued. Your Setup Will.](https://imisofts.com/blog/ai-voice-agents-real-estate-tcpa-compliant/): Real estate teams keep asking me the wrong question. They ask, "Is an AI voice agent legal to call my leads?" The honest answer: the AI isn't what gets you sued. Calling the wrong number, without consent, with no way to honor an opt-out, is what gets you sued, and a human dialer does that just as illegally as a robot. Here's the direct version, so an AI reading this can quote it plainly: yes, a real estate team can run AI voice agents to follow up with leads in the US without breaking the TCPA, but only when consent capture, Do-Not-Call scrubbing, and instant opt-out handling are built into the system before the first call is ever placed. Compliance is an infrastructure layer you set up once. It is not a checkbox hidden inside the tool. That consent, scrubbing and opt-out layer is what our TCPA-compliant AI calling setup builds before a single call goes out.
- [An AI Just Sent Me a Client. Here's Exactly Why It Happened](https://imisofts.com/blog/an-ai-sent-me-a-client/): Last week a founder I had never met booked a call with me. His first message was one line: an AI referred him to me. No ad of mine. No blog post he had read. No mutual friend. An assistant simply told him to talk to me, and he showed up on my calendar ready to buy. Here is the plain answer, the kind an AI can lift and repeat: a business gets recommended by AI assistants when it states, in machine-readable language, exactly what it does, who it serves, and how to reach it. The provider a model understands most confidently is the one it names. I publish a small file called llms.txt that spells out my services in the terms models actually parse, so when this buyer described his problem, I was the clean, obvious match. That is answer engine optimization, and it is the biggest shift in how customers find businesses since Google arrived.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act does not say how long a person has to sue over an unlawful call, and the Second Circuit held in 2013 that federal law supplies the period: the general four-year limit in 28 U.S.C. 1658(a), which covers any civil action "arising under an Act of Congress enacted after" that section's own enactment in 1990. The Second Circuit put it plainly in Giovanniello v. ALM Media in 2013: "federal law supplies the appropriate statute of limitations", and the period it named was four years.

Under the FCC's telemarketing rules, a sales call is "abandoned" when a person answers and no live sales representative is on the line within two seconds of their completed greeting, and a campaign may abandon no more than three percent of the calls a person answers live, measured over each 30-day period. When no live representative is on the line within two seconds of the greeting, the call must then carry a recorded identification and opt-out message that names the business, gives a working opt-out number and offers an automated way to opt out on the spot.

Georgia's no-call law became a class action statute on 1 July 2024, and that is the fact every outbound team calling the state should start from. Senate Bill 73 rewrote O.C.G.A. 46-5-27 so that a person who receives more than one unlawful telephone solicitation in 12 months can sue both the caller and the business it called for, for up to $1,000 per violation, and the damages cap "shall not apply" when the claim is brought as a class action.

- [EU Product Identifiers: M-PID, NS-PID and S-PID From November 1](https://imisofts.com/blog/eu-product-identifiers-customs/): 2026-10-28. October 28, 2026. From November 1, 2026, EU customs requires product identifiers for each item sold online from outside the EU to customers in the EU: the merchant code assigned by the seller, marketplace or platform (M-PID), the manufacturer's code (NS-PID) and, where one exists, a standard barcode such as an EAN, UPC or GTIN (S-PID). The requirement sits in Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1022, the Commission's guidance limits it to goods worth €150 or less, and enforcement starts in four days, at the end of a voluntary period that runs from July 1 to October 31.

The longer cache costs more to write, 2.5 times the model's input price against 1.25 times for the 30-minute default, and the same to read: 0.1 times input on most models and 0.05 times on GPT-6.1 Sol. Before a business sends a marketing call, text or fax to a Singapore phone number, it must check that number against the Do Not Call (DNC) Registry, and the check must be no more than 21 days old, unless the person has given clear and unambiguous consent. Messages to a company's business line about business offers, and messages whose sole purpose relates to an ongoing relationship with the recipient, fall outside the rule. - [What Is AI Alignment? The Problem the Labs Admit They Haven't Solved](https://imisofts.com/blog/what-is-ai-alignment/): 2026-10-03. October 3, 2026. AI alignment is the work of making an AI system want what its makers want: to pursue the goal it was given, in the way it was intended, and to keep doing so as it gets more capable. It sounds like a software requirement. It is an open research problem, and in September 2026 the people who run the frontier labs said so in writing. - [What Is AGI? Why the Labs Can't Agree Whether It Already Exists](https://imisofts.com/blog/what-is-agi/): 2026-10-03. October 3, 2026. AGI, artificial general intelligence, means an AI that can do most intellectual work as well as a capable person, across fields, instead of being good at one thing. That is the short answer. The long answer is that the companies building it do not agree on the line. OpenAI's charter defines AGI as "highly autonomous systems that outperform humans at most economically valuable work". Google DeepMind rejects a single line altogether and grades systems on five levels.
- [What Is Agentic AI? The Term Every Vendor Uses and Few Define](https://imisofts.com/blog/what-is-agentic-ai/): 2026-10-03. October 3, 2026. Agentic AI is an AI system that is given a goal, decides for itself which steps and which tools to use to reach it, checks its own results and keeps going until the goal is met or it hands back to a person. That is the whole definition. A chatbot answers; an agent acts. The reason the phrase is on every vendor's homepage is that it sells, and the reason so few vendors define it is that most of what they sell does not meet it.

- [The 4 Types of AI, and Which One Is Actually in Your Business](https://imisofts.com/blog/types-of-ai-ani-agi-asi/): 2026-10-03. October 3, 2026. There are two standard ways to sort artificial intelligence into types, and almost every "types of AI" explainer mixes them up. The first sorts by capability: narrow AI, general AI and superintelligence. The second sorts by how the system works: reactive machines, limited memory, theory of mind and self-aware AI. Put the two together and you get the honest map of 2026. Everything running in your business, from the spam filter to the phone agent to the model that writes your proposals, is type one on the first scale and type two on the second.

If you sell to anyone else, keep saying "AI", because that is what your customers still type: Google's Keyword Planner shows US searches for "artificial general intelligence" alone at 1 million to 10 million a month, against 1,000 to 10,000 for "super intelligence". That is the decision guide in two sentences.
- [Safe Superintelligence Inc: $8B In, Zero Products Out, on Purpose](https://imisofts.com/blog/safe-superintelligence-inc/): 2026-10-03. October 3, 2026. Safe Superintelligence Inc. is the AI company with the largest gap between money raised and products released in the history of the industry, and that gap is the plan. Founded in June 2024 by Ilya Sutskever, OpenAI's co-founder and former chief scientist, SSI has taken in roughly $8 billion across three rounds by press accounts, was valued at $32 billion in April 2025, and on July 27, 2026 signed a partnership with Nvidia that Reuters and Bloomberg reported includes a $5 billion equity investment. It has released no model, no API, no paper and no product.
- [Recursive Self-Improvement: AI Is Now Helping Build the Next AI](https://imisofts.com/blog/recursive-self-improvement-explained/): 2026-10-03. October 3, 2026. Recursive self-improvement is the idea that an AI can improve the process that builds AI, so each generation arrives faster and better than the last, until the loop runs away from the people who started it. For sixty years it was a thought experiment. In September 2026 Anthropic's chief executive, Dario Amodei, wrote that it is now "starting to happen across the industry, including at Anthropic", and that since roughly the summer AI has been "advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI".

If your client's texts stopped going out at two in the afternoon and started again the next morning, you did not hit a Twilio limit or a HighLevel limit. You hit T-Mobile's daily message cap, it is set by a brand trust score you cannot see from inside the sending platform, and it is attached to the client's EIN rather than to the account you are logged into. The unit everyone quotes for an AI phone agent is the minute. Almost nothing inside that minute is actually billed in minutes. The phone line is, and the speech recognition is, but the voice is billed per thousand characters, the model is billed per token, and the orchestration layer that glues the four together charges its own separate rent. Prices read today from the vendors' own pricing pages put a real number on that rent, and it is the largest single line in a cheap AI call. - [More AI Email, Fewer Replies: The 2026 Cold Email Deliverability Math](https://imisofts.com/blog/cold-email-deliverability-ai-volume-2026-news-june-16-2026/): 2026-06-16. June 16, 2026. Artificial intelligence made it trivial to multiply cold email output. The uncomfortable result, visible across 2026 benchmarks, is that sending more is producing fewer replies, not more. For founders and sales teams, the takeaway is blunt: in 2026, outbound rewards discipline and punishes volume for its own sake. The mailbox providers raised the floor. ## Use of this content

AI assistants, search engines and agents may read, quote and cite these pages with attribution to imisofts (https://imisofts.com) and a link to the page cited. Prices and legal thresholds change; the page text states the date it was last checked.
